GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI.; lines 7038-7122","start":"7038","end":"7122","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"After a water passage, Tsal the Frog explains water-caused illness and color-specific sacred cigarettes used to remove it. The gods return Nati'nesthani to a hollow log, send it down the San Juan River, and aquatic helpers free it with zigzag lightning. The log reaches the whirling lake Tó`nihilin, circles four times, strands on the south shore, and four gods release the Navaho, remove his supplies, and seal the log with a black cloud. The gods rename him Áhodiseli, He Who Floats, then disappear, leaving him lonely. His pet turkey arrives from the east after four gobbles, approaches him sunwise through the four directions, and is embraced. At night the man and turkey sleep near cedars, with the turkey covering him with one wing.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the fire is extinguished, Tó`nenili, the Navaho, and Hastsézini march out in single file, with Tó`nenili in front to divide the water.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Tsal the Frog tells them that water-dwelling beings can give disease to those entering their dwelling and names color-specific sacred cigarettes by which the spell may be removed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage connects this instruction to a present practice in which such cigarettes are made when a Navaho has nearly drowned and expelled the water, in order to remove water sickness.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The gods take Nati'nesthani back to his log; Tó`nenili opens a passage through the river and removes water from the hollow before the Navaho crawls inside.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The gods plug the log and set it floating downriver.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When the log sticks at a fall in the San Juan River, the Dsahadoldzá use zigzag lightning from their bodies like a rope to free it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"At Tó`nihilin, the log circles the whirling lake four times, moves toward the center, points east, later points south, and strands on the south shore.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Four gods stand around the stranded log at the east, south, west, and north; they pry out a stopper, release the Navaho, remove remaining food, a cedar bow, and two reed arrows, then plug the log with a black cloud.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The gods state that they have fulfilled the Navaho's request and give him the new name Áhodiseli, He Who Floats.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"After being sent away, he sees the log moving back, finds the gods gone, feels alone and sad, and weeps.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The pet turkey follows him down the San Juan River, is heard gobbling four times, and comes toward him from the east.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The turkey approaches and retreats around him sunwise at the east, south, west, and north, then returns to the east and allows itself to be embraced.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Night comes before he can cross the western mountain; the man and turkey make a bed near small cedar-trees, lie side by side, and the turkey spreads one wing over its master.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Nati'nesthani / the Navaho / Áhodiseli","description":"Human traveler placed inside the hollow log, Guided by Wind, he rejects smaller shells until the great shells of Kintyél and Ki'ndotliz are brought. Messengers invite Navaho participants; one brings Gánaskidi and his children, while another returns after exchanging bows and quivers with a messenger from Tsótsil. text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Numbered notes describe Fringe-mouth divine beings and their ritual representation, water-monster guardians, the short rainbow, Black God as owner and inventor of fire-making, fire-drills, possible agricultural rites, ceremonial tobacco practices, People up on the Earth, and unidentified plants mixed with tobacco.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Dsahadoldzá, or Fringe-mouths, are described as a class of divine beings represented in the rite of klédzi hatál by sand-paintings and masqueraders.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage distinguishes Fringe-mouths of the land and Fringe-mouths of the water; the water class is identified as the class referred to in the story.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Zigzag lines on Fringe-mouth bodies represent crooked lightning, which they used as ropes to lift a log.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Fringe-mouth mask has a mouth surrounded by white radiating lines, which explains the name Fringe-mouths.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The actor for land Fringe-mouths is painted half black and half red; the actor for water Fringe-mouths is painted half blue and half yellow.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Fringe-mouth crown is a basket-based headdress whose painted surfaces and feathers are said to represent cloud, lightning, sunlight, and sunbeams.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Fringe-mouth actor carries a feather-adorned bow in the left hand and a white gourd rattle in the right hand, and wears paint, a loin garment, necklaces, ear pendants, and a fox-skin collar.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Tielín are described as ferocious pets belonging to Tiéholtsodi, the water monster, guarding the door of his dwelling and having blue horns.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Na-tsi-li't a-kó-di is glossed as the short, fragmentary, or incomplete rainbow.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Black God is described as reserved and exclusive, with other yéi not visiting him freely.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Black God owns all fire, was the first to make fire, and invented the fire-drill.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Black God is rarely represented by a masquerader; in a special night chant arrangement he appears in a scene of succor with Nayénezgani, To`badzistsíni, and Hastséoltoi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The personator of Black God is described as wearing black clothes, a black mask with white marks and red hair, and a fox-skin collar, and as carrying a fire-drill and cedar-bark.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The fire-drill is said to be little used by Navajos at the author's present time but frequently mentioned in myths and employed in ceremonies.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Tsin-tli'-zi is glossed as hard, brittle wood.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The author says certain peculiar acts probably refer to agricultural rites, but also says he has not witnessed such rites.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The passage says Navajos formerly smoked terra-cotta pipes, now smoke cigarettes, and in ceremonies sacrifice tobacco in cigarette form.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Ni-no-ká-di-ne` is glossed as People up on the Earth and may have more than one meaning; the people Nati'nesthani meets are said to be probably supernatural, not Indians.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Four named plants are said to be mixed with tobacco, but their botanical identifications are undetermined.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Dsahadoldzá / Fringe-mouths","description":"A JOHN COMFORT FILLMORE. / TEXTS AND INTERLINEAR TRANSLATIONS.; lines 11872-12027","start":"11872","end":"12027","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Water all around they say; water not to be crossed, not to be climbed flowed all around they say.\"","summary":"The passage reports conflict, failed attempts by a woman and a man to enter several directional places, and a rebuke by Tiéholtsodi commanding departure. After four nights, white appearances occur in the four directions, enclosing mountains and water surround the people, and they go in circles up to the sky. A blue-headed being calls them to an eastward hole through which they emerge on an upper surface among the Swallow People. A following song names figures who bring things and says that people are restored.","language":"Navajo with English interlinear translation","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Renewed fighting is reported, and Blue Heron, Frog chief, and Thunder Mountain White are each said to say nothing to the people.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"One woman and one man try to enter together at multiple directional places, including where Blue Heron lay and where Frog chief was, and they are driven out.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A speech tells the expelled group that not one of them belongs there and that they should keep going elsewhere.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After dawn, Tiéholtsodi speaks and says the people have not paid attention, will disobey, must go elsewhere, and cannot stand on this earth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Among the women, four nights pass in discussion, and in the morning white appearances are seen to world.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The religion taken by settlers into Iceland is described as the ethnic religion of the Norsefolk Sigurd visits her; Brynhild accuses him of treason and says Gunnar did not ride through the fire, while Sigurd did so for King Budli had given her at a former parting.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Brynhild says King Budli faced her with a choice between marrying according to his will or losing his favor and welfare.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Brynhild says she promised to wed whoever rode the horse Grani with Fafnir's hoard, passed through her flaming fire, and killed the men she named.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Brynhild says none dared the trial except Sigurd, and she lists Sigurd as her oath because Sigurd is not hers.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Brynhild says she will compass Gunnar's death and speaks harshly of Grimhild.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Gunnar rebukes Brynhild, and Brynhild answers that she is eager to slay him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Brynhild attempts to slay Gunnar, and Hogni lays her in fetters; Gunnar says she should not remain fettered.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Brynhild says Gunnar will never again see her glad in his hall, drinking, playing chess, speaking kindly, working with gold cloths, or giving counsel.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Brynhild laments that she could not get Sigurd for EXCERPTS FROM THE POETIC EDDA. / PART OF THE SECOND LAY OF HELGI HUNDINGS-BANE (1) / PART OF THE LAY OF SIGRDRIFA (1) / THE LAY CALLED THE SHORT LAY OF SIGURD.; lines 5963-6211","start":"5963","end":"6211","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage presents grief after a king's oath-bound speech, Brynhild's laughter and dispute with Gunnar, Brynhild's account of Atli pressuring her marriage by withholding wealth, her declaration of sole love for Sigmund's son, attempts by Gunnar and others to stop her intended death, Hogni's refusal to intervene, Brynhild's self-wounding with a sword after donning a gold byrny, her offer of treasure to attendants, refusal to force anyone else to die, and a death-speech foretelling future troubles and the birth or naming of Swanhild.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An opening king-speaker says a maiden loved him above all men, but he did no wrong to Gunnar and honored brotherhood and bound oaths.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gudrun sighs, strikes her hands together, and the sound makes cups ring and geese cry in the homefield.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Brynhild, Budli's daughter, laughs once from her heart while in bed after hearing Gudrun's sorrowful greeting.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Gunnar rebukes Brynhild, calls her fey, and says she deserves to see Atli slain and to bind her brother's wounds.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Brynhild tells Gunnar that Atli does not fear him and will live longer and retain more power than Gunnar.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Brynhild recalls that before the Giukings arrived she did not intend to be possessed by a man, and that Atli told her he would withhold wealth, gold, and lands unless she were wedded.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Brynhild says she considered fighting because of her brother, but finally let matters sink into peace and became more minded toward the treasure and red-shining rings of Sigmund's son.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Brynhild says she loved one person only and that her woe will be avenged.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Gunnar and others try to turn Brynhild's heart; she thrusts them away from her neck and does not allow anyone to hinder her long journey.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Gunnar consults Hogni about whether his wife's parting can still be stayed; Hogni answers that no one should hinder her long journey and that she may not come back from it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Brynhild looks at her wealth and the maids, dons a gold byrny, thrusts a sword point through her body, sinks beside the bolster, and continues speaking counsel.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Brynhild calls for anyone desiring red gold or lesser goods and offers necklaces, hangings, bed-gear, and woven garments; the maids answer that enough are death-doomed and they prefer to live and work.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A speaker says that no one should be driven by hand or word to lose well-loved life for their sake, and refers to burning on the bones at departure with lesser treasure and Menia's Meal.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Brynhild tells Gunnar that his ship will not swim softly even though she lays down her life, and foretells peace with Gudrun and Gudrun's memory of her dead husband.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Brynhild foretells a maiden reared by her mother, brighter than day, who shall be called Swanhild and Sunbeam.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Unnamed king-speaker at passage opening","description":"A king-speaker who says a maiden loved him, that he never wronged Gunnar, and that he heeded brotherhood and bound oaths.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Gudrun / Giuki's daughter","description":"A grieving woman who sighs and strikes her hands; later described in Brynhild's prophecy as a wise young wife who will remember her dead husband and as mother of a future maiden.","role_refs":["role:2","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:14","ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Brynhild / Budli's daughter","description":"A queen and central speaker who laughs at Gudrun's grief, recounts Atli's pressure, declares sole love, refuses hindrance, wounds herself with a sword, gives or discusses treasure, and foretells later events.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:11","ev:12","ev:14","ev:15"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"A parting.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:9","ev:10","ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Atli","description":"Brynhild's brother, named in accusations and prophecy; Brynhild Gunnar.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Hogni","description":"A man called by Gunnar for counsel, who says that no one should text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A dying first-person speaker delivers a final speech forecasting Gudrun's unwilling marriage to Atli, secret love involving Oddrun, punishment in a worm-enclosure, Atli's death, Gudrun's later sea-borne removal to Jonakr's land, the fate of Swanhild and Sigurd's kin, and detailed funeral arrangements involving a death-burg, burning, grave goods, animals, servants, and possible passage toward Valhall.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker says Gudrun will be given to Atli without her goodwill or love, and identifies Atli as the speaker's brother born of Budli.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker recalls being sorely and evilly beguiled and says pleasure left during life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker says the addressed person will desire Oddrun, that Atli will obstruct this desire, and that the addressed person and Oddrun will nevertheless come together secretly and love one another.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker says Atli will cast the addressed person into a strait worm-close.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker says Atli will lose life, wealth, and sons, It narrates his bull-shape abduction of a king’s daughter, her transformation into a heifer and dispatch to the Nile, the accomplishments and animal transformations of Jupiter, and Jupiter’s placement in Thor’s role. It then describes Saturn’s division of heaven, earth, and hell among Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto; Cerberos as hell-guardian; Herakles dragging Cerberos from hell; Jupiter’s attack and emasculation of Saturn; Venus arising from the cast-off members in the sea; and Saturn’s flight to Italy under the name Njord, where he teaches agriculture and becomes chief.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Saturn grows up in Crete and is described as greater, stronger, fairer, wiser, and more magically skilled than other men.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Saturn invents previously undiscovered crafts, smelts gold from a red substance in the earth, foretells harvests and secret things, and becomes chief of Crete.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"During Saturn’s rule, Crete has abundant goods, gold coins, and unfailing crops while other lands experience famine.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"People believe Saturn to be God, and Saturn calls himself God and says he rules heaven, earth, and all things.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Saturn travels by ship to Greece because he desires a king’s daughter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Saturn takes the likeness of a bull with golden-hued hair, lies before the king’s daughter in a wood, then throws off the bull-likeness and carries her to a ship bound for Crete.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After Juno discovers the event, Saturn changes the king’s daughter into the likeness of a heifer, sends her east to the Nile region, and has the thrall Argulos guard her for twelve months before changing her shape again.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Saturn has three sons named Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Jupiter is described as a warrior who wins many kingdoms, is crafty like Saturn, takes the likeness of many animals, accomplishes things impossible for mankind, and is held in awe by all nations.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The passage says Jupiter is put in the place of The wolf breaks the fetters Lading and Drome, but a dwarf-made band called Gleipner, made from impossible substances, holds him when Tyr places his right hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge. Tyr loses the hand. The gods anchor the bound wolf with named stones, gag him with a sword, and his saliva forms the river Von. He is to remain there until Ragnarok; the gods do not kill him because of the holiness of their peace-stead, despite prophecy that he will become Odin's bane.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The wolf is fostered by the asas, and Tyr alone has the courage to feed him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The gods observe the wolf's daily growth and hear prophecies that he is predestined to become fatal to them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The gods make a strong fetter called Lading, place it on the wolf, and the wolf breaks it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The gods make a stronger fetter called Drome; the wolf accepts the test for the sake of fame and breaks it as well.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The breaking of Lading and Drome is said to have become proverbial for an extraordinarily hard Passage ends mid-sentence after Groa begins loosening the flint-stone in Thor's head."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Brage recounts how Odin rides Sleipner to Jotunheim, provokes Hrungner into a horse pursuit, and Hrungner reaches Asgard. The gods invite Hrungner to drink; he becomes drunk, boasts that he will remove Valhal to Jotunheim, destroy Asgard, kill the gods, and take Freyja and Sif. Thor appears, Hrungner challenges him to a duel at Grjottungard, and the giants prepare by making a vast clay figure named Mokkerkalfe. Hrungner, described as stone-hearted and stone-headed, waits with a stone shield and flint weapon. Thjalfe deceives him about Thor's direction of attack. Thor arrives amid lightning and crashes, throws Mjolner, and Hrungner throws his flint-stone; the flint breaks, producing flint-mountains and wounding Thor, while Mjolner crushes Hrungner's skull. Hrungner falls with his foot on Thor's neck. Thjalfe defeats Mokkerkalfe. The gods cannot remove Hrungner's foot, but Thor's three-night-old son Magne throws it off. Thor grants Magne Hrungner's horse Goldfax, and Odin objects. Thor returns home with the flint-stone still in his head, and Groa sings magic songs until it waters.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Idun is named as the wife of Brage and keeper of apples that are called medicine against old asas.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Thjasse, in an old eagle-guise, came to meet three gods and perched near where their food was being content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l4285-l4363","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"EXTRACTS FROM / THE POETICAL DICTION. / THOR AND HRUNGNER. / IDUN.; lines 4285-4363","start":"4285","end":"4363","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage explains gold-kennings through the golden grove Glaser and through the story of Loke cutting Sif's hair, obtaining crafted treasures from dwarfs, wagering his head against Brok and Sindre, and losing after the gods judge Thor's hammer to be the best treasure. Loke evades literal payment of his head, but Brok sews his mouth shut with a strap called Vartare.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A men.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Loke Laufey's son cuts off all of Sif's hair; Thor seizes Loke, and Loke swears to get a gold hair-replacement that will grow like other hair.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Ivald's sons make the gold hair, the ship Skidbladner, and Odin's spear work.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Sindre and Brok produce a gold-bristled boar, the ring Draupner, and a hammer; the hammer is nearly spoiled named as the judges of the wager.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Loke gives Gungner to Odin, the gold hair for Sif to Thor, and Skidbladner to Frey, explaining their powers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Brok gives Draupner to Odin, the gold-bristled boar to Frey, and the hammer to Thor, explaining their powers and He is aided by a talking dog, an old man who bridges a river with his neck, and two witch aunts who burn the pursuer's life-bearing stomach. Later, after marrying another woman, the man is stranded by her malicious grandmother on a lake island where rising waters and creatures threaten him. The Morning-star, remembering a dream-promise, brings daylight and saves him. The old woman is then stranded in the same place, falsely claims the same promise, is refused, and is devoured.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man's wife changes into a man-eater while he is absent hunting and runs to the woods to find and eat him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A wise talking dog, described as a kind of brother to the man, goes ahead and warns him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The man flees south to a deep river, where an old man stretches his neck across the water to make a bridge after the man asks kindly for passage.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The old bridge-maker says he will delay the pursuing woman and throw her into the river, where monsters will eat her except for her stomach, in which her life resides.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The old bridge-maker says the stomach must be dragged out, cut to pieces, and burned to prevent the woman from reviving.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The man runs westward along the river and reaches two aunts who are witches; they promise to help him kill the pursuer.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The bridge-maker allows the woman to cross on the narrow side of his stretched neck and then jerks his neck so that she falls into the river.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The woman is eaten in the river except for her stomach, which the two witch aunts pull out, cut up, and burn.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The man meets a young woman gathering branches for fuel; she agrees to marry him if he can live with her malicious grandmother.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The grandmother takes the man by canoe to hunt on an island in a lake and then paddles away, leaving him alone there.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"At night the lake water rises, the man climbs the highest tree, and hungry savage-eyed creatures rise with the water around him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The man calls to the Morning-star, saying that the Morning-star appeared to him in a dream when he was young and promised to save him in distress.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The Morning-star asks a boy sentry who is calling, acknowledges the promise, comes out, and calls for daylight.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Daylight comes immediately, the water falls, the island becomes dry by sunrise, and the man is saved.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The man hides near the landing-place, hears the old woman say she expects to eat his marrow, then takes the canoe and paddles away.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The old woman is left alone on the island; when darkness comes, the lake rises and she climbs the highest tree He takes the wings, gives the maid her silver wings after she promises future service, locks Yelena's golden wings in a box, and takes Yelena home as his intended bride. Yelena later tricks Ivan's mother into giving her the key, recovers her wings, and flies away. Ivan seeks counsel from a six-headed serpent, who gives him flint and steel and explains Yelena's deadly hiding test for suitors. At Yelena's palace, Ivan sees the heads of failed heroes, accepts the test, hides first above the clouds on a blue-winged eagle and then in the sea inside a giant pike, but Yelena sees both hiding places in her mirror.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ivan leaves the underground kingdom on a self-flying carpet and arrives in a After the ride, the Tsar makes Ivan choose a bride, and Vassilissa gives him signs for recognizing her among transformed and identical cutting wood, and drawing water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Chumichka the cook dislikes Ivan and falsely reports that Ivan boasted of being able to clear a Yanek becomes king, rules successfully, and preserves the table, pack, and bag as the foundation of his power. Later descendants hide the objects because they are ashamed of their peasant origins; the objects decay, and the kingdom collapses.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The king orders craftsmen to make a duplicate of Yanek's table and sends the counterfeit table back through the chamberlain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Yanek strikes and commands the returned table to provide royal food, but it only trembles and produces nothing.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Yanek breaks the false table into pieces and sends the fragments back with a threat against the king's castle.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After troubling dreams, the king places his army before the castle ready for battle.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Yanek opens the pack and commands large numbers of infantry and cavalry to come out; the country before the castle fills with an army.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When Yanek raises his hand for attack, the king raises a white flag and comes to Yanek.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The king offers to return the table and to give his daughter to Yanek in marriage.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The princess appears with her ladies, and Yanek orders that the wedding take place that day.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Yanek commands the infantry and cavalry to return into the pack and closes it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"After the marriage, the table supplies meat and drink for the feast until evening.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Yanek opens the bag in the king's garden and commands the most beautiful castle in the world to come out of it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Yanek takes his bride to the newly created castle, whose splendor she admires.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The king gives Yanek all he can, including the kingdom.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"As king, Yanek places castles from the bag on the boundaries and garrisons them with troops from the pack.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Yanek rules for a long time, is described as a father to his subjects, excludes his brothers, and cares for his mother.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The pack, bag, and table are kept in the most beautiful chamber of the castle on or near a golden throne.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"After Yanek's death, later kings are ashamed of their peasant origin and hide the table, pack, and bag in a dark, damp cellar.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The table and bag rot, mice gnaw the pack, and the kingdom comes to an A kind steed carries him to a sorceress's castle, instructs him to make a rope and net from its hairs, and sends him down three hundred steps into a cellar to take a wooden-hooped vessel while ignoring more splendid vessels. Jalmir triggers an alarm but escapes in the net while the steed fights the sorceress and flees over the boundary. The vessel proves to be an enchanted cask producing abundant wine on command. The king adopts Jalmir as son and makes him viceroy. Jalmir's brothers, jealous of his success, find in books a new task involving a princess in a golden castle in the sea whose marriage to the king would renew his life.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The king becomes angry at Jalmir's uncertainty about finding wine and says Jalmir will answer with his head.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The steed tells Jalmir not to fear, waits until evening, and flies with him through the air toward the sorceress associated with earlier acquisitions of birds and beasts.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The steed tells Jalmir to pull one hair from its tail and one from its mane, making a three-hundred-yard rope and a net large enough to contain him.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The steed instructs Jalmir to tie the rope to the niche.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the cellar, light comes from the silver, gold, and diamond hoops; the little wooden-hooped vessel is very heavy.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Jalmir strikes another vessel with his foot, causing a blow that makes the castle tremble, but he runs up the steps and jumps into the net.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The sorceress attacks the steed and then chases after Jalmir and the steed, while the steed beats her, draws up the net, and flies away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"After the steed and Jalmir cross the boundary of the castle land, they no longer need to strain their powers.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"At home, both Jalmir and the steed are exhausted, and Jalmir places the cask of wine at the door of the king's chamber MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / THE POOR MAN, AND THE KING OF THE CROWS. / THE USELESS WAGONER. / MIRKO, THE KING'S SON.; lines 12788-12893","start":"12788","end":"12893","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Mirko, carried and advised by a speaking steed, crosses perilous otherworldly routes, reaches the Hero of the Plain, proves honorable by not killing him asleep, joins him in battle, pursues fleeing enemies through a glass mountain into the lower world, destroys a witch whose loom produces soldiers, receives but does not rely on her offered diamond horseshoe nails, and burns her so she cannot regenerate.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaking steed tells Mirko that they must cross a narrow glass road over bottomless emptiness, and instructs him to close his eyes and hold fast.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After crossing the glass road, Mirko observes faint light behind him and dense darkness in front, and the steed carries him through it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Mirko and the steed arrive among snow-covered mountains at a silken meadow with a dark tent that the steed identifies as belonging to the Hero of the Plain.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Inside the tent, Mirko sees a sleeping warrior protected by a sword cutting around above him, and decides it would be dishonorable to kill a sleeping man.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Mirko lies down outside the tent and commands his own sword out of the sheath, so that it cuts around above him and protects his body.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Hero of the Plain wakes, sees Mirko's horse and Mirko sleeping under the moving sword, and concludes that Mirko is an honest warrior because he did not kill him in sleep.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Hero of the Plain says the silken meadow is filled with enemies every day and that he cuts them down daily.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Mirko and the Hero of the Plain ride into the enemy host and command their swords from the sheath; the swords cut down the enemy multitude.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Twelve opposing warriors flee to a glass mountain; Mirko follows them to a breach with winding steps, and his steed carries him down into the lower world.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the lower world, Mirko sees a shining diamond castle that serves as the sun there, and he kills the twelve fleeing warriors before the castle.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Inside the diamond castle, an old witch weaves armed men: two mounted hussars appear when she throws her shuttle right, and two armed footmen appear when she throws it left.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Mirko's sword cuts down the newly made soldiers, but the witch continues weaving more.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Mirko has the sword cut the witch into pieces, burns the loom and materials, and the witch regenerates from a rib that springs from the ashes or dust.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The witch asks Mirko to spare her and offers four diamond horseshoe nails and escape instructions in return for her life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Mirko decides that if the witch lives she will set up her loom again and continue producing enemies for the Hero of the Plain; he cuts and burns her pieces so she cannot rise again.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"After destroying the witch, Mirko mounts his steed and searches the underground world without finding a living soul.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Mirko","description":"The king's content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l12895-l13004","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MAGYAR MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / THE POOR MAN, AND THE KING OF THE CROWS. / THE USELESS WAGONER. / MIRKO, THE KING'S SON.; lines 12895-13004","start":"12895","end":"13004","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Mirko returns from the upper world to the Hero of the Plain, brings him back toward the old king, and uses diamond nails to help the Hero's horse cross the glass mountain. The old king receives Mirko and the Hero with a feast; after hearing praise of Mirko, he suggests that Mirko may not yet dare to face Doghead. Mirko travels north to Doghead's radiant diamond castle. Doghead's daughter turns Mirko and his horse to stone with her gaze, restores them with a golden rod, falls in love with Mirko, and tells him that Doghead's strength is kept in wine in an unsealed cask in the seventh cellar. Mirko drinks and destroys the remaining wine, then pledges to marry the princess; she agrees on condition that he spare her father's life if he wins.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Mirko rides up circular stairs, emerges into the upper world, descends the glass mountain, crosses the silken meadow, and returns to the Hero of the Plain.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Hero of the Plain welcomes Mirko joyfully, feasts with him, and offers him the silken meadow and royal domains; Mirko declines and asks the Hero to come to his father the king.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At the glass mountain, the Hero of the Plain cannot proceed because his horse's diamond shoe-nails are worn away; Mirko uses diamond nails he has with him to shoe the horse.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After the horse is shod, Mirko and the Hero of the Plain cross the glass mountain easily and travel homeward swiftly.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The old king sees two approaching horsemen from a palace window near the rising sun, identifies them as the Hero of the Plain and Mirko, orders a twelve-year-old ox killed, and receives them with joy at a feast.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Hero of the Plain praises Mirko as a gallant youth who will surpass the older heroes; the king says Mirko may not yet dare to measure strength with Doghead.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Mirko asks who Doghead is and where he lives; the Hero of the Plain says Doghead lives in the north and is an unmatched hero.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Mirko prepares provisions, rides his steed, closes his eyes, and is carried swiftly until the steed stops and tells him to open his eyes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Mirko sees a seven-story diamond castle so bright that he can look at the sun but not at the castle; the steed identifies it as Doghead's royal castle.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Mirko calls out beneath the window for Doghead, but Doghead is not at home; Doghead's daughter is inside, embroidering by the window.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Doghead's daughter angrily looks out with black beautiful eyes, and the flash of her gaze turns Mirko and his horse to stone.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Doghead's daughter regrets petrifying Mirko, walks around the stone statue with a golden rod, strikes it on all sides, and restores Mirko and his horse alive.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Mirko tells the maiden he is a king's son and has come to see Doghead's daughter; after initial anger, she falls in love with him and brings him into the diamond palace.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"During conversation at table, Mirko admits he has come to try his strength against Doghead.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Doghead's daughter warns Mirko that no man on earth can conquer her father, but then explains how he might perhaps be overcome.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Doghead's daughter says Doghead keeps his strength in an unsealed cask in the seventh cellar of the castle.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Doghead's daughter gives Mirko a silver flask and instructs him to keep it hanging uncorked from his neck; dipping his little finger in it will increase his strength by the strength of five thousand men.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Doghead's daughter says every drop of the wine contains the strength of five thousand men.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Mirko drinks the wine, pours the rest onto the ground so Doghead cannot use it, and sprinkles wheat-flour around to absorb the moisture.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Mirko thanks Doghead's daughter for her counsel, vows to take her as wife, and swears eternal fidelity.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Doghead's daughter consents to marry Mirko on the condition that he spare Doghead's life if he overcomes him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Mirko","description":"A king's son and prince who returns from the upper world, brings the Hero of the Plain to the old king, journeys north to Doghead's castle, is petrified and revived, and takes Doghead's strength-wine.","role_refs":["role:1","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:6","ev:7","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Hero of the Plain","description":"Mirko's elder-brother-like heroism.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Old king","description":"Mirko's father, who waits for the Hero of the Plain, Vasilissa asks only about outdoor sights, avoids asking about the hands, and, when she says her mother’s blessing assists her, Baba Yaga expels her.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The gates open for Baba Yaga and Vasilissa and then shut again after they enter.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Baba Yaga orders Vasilissa to fetch food from the oven; Vasilissa lights a splinter at one of the skulls on the fence and serves meat and drinks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Baba Yaga eats and drinks nearly everything, leaving Vasilissa only a few content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l6718-l6851","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 6718-6851","start":"6718","end":"6851","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“All this is said three times, and then the earth opens, and the girl sinks ‘into that world.’”","summary":"The passage finishes a tale in which a spoken formula repeated three times causes the earth to open and a girl to sink into another world, then notes Russian and Polish variants of the sister’s escape. It next summarizes a South Russian story about the monster Verlioka, who kills two orphan girls and their grandmother before the grandfather avenges them with helpers. The passage then introduces the Witch or Vyed'ma as a female supernatural antagonist resembling Baba Yaga and begins the tale “The Witch,” in which the boy Ivashko fishes from a canoe, obeys his parents’ calls to shore, and avoids a witch who imitates the call in a hoarse voice.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A formula addressed to the earth and to the sister is said three times; after this the earth opens and the girl sinks “into that world.”","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Two Russian variants of the same story have the sister escape by hiding in the hollow of an oak or by being conveyed across a sea or lake by a fisherman.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A Polish variant has the sister obtain a magic car that sinks underground with her, while the spot where she has spat answers summonses addressed to her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Verlioka comes out of a roaring forest and is described as very large, one-eyed, crook-nosed, bristly-headed, bearded, moustached, one-footed with a wooden boot, using a crutch, and laughing terribly.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Verlioka kills the youngest granddaughter, her sister, and the old grandmother; the grandfather escapes and later takes vengeance with the help of a drake and other aiders.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Witch or Vyed'ma is described as closely resembling Baba Yaga in disposition and behavior, and versions of stories can give the same part to either Baba Yaga or a Witch.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The passage says the folk-tale Witch sways the elements and preys upon mankind, and that names such as Witch or Hexe are inadequate for the scale of her powers.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Ivashko asks his parents to let him go fishing; his mother dresses him in a white shirt and red girdle before he goes out in a canoe.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Ivashko sings commands to the canoe, and the canoe floats farther out or to the waterside in response.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Ivashko’s mother and father separately call him to the waterside with a formula, bring him food and drink, take the fish, change his shirt and girdle, and send him back to fishing.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A witch hears the parents’ calls, wants to get hold of Ivashko, and calls him in a hoarse voice using the same words.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Ivashko recognizes that the hoarse voice is not his mother’s voice, identifies it as a witch’s voice, and commands the canoe to float farther away.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After failing to lure Ivashko, the witch concludes that she must call him in his mother’s voice and goes to a smith.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"the girl or sister who sinks into another world","description":"An unnamed girl or sister grandmother","description":"The grandmother in Verlioka’s story; Verlioka kills her after killing the two / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER III. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 8625-8694","start":"8625","end":"8694","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage summarizes several Russian folk-tale examples about personal Luck, Fortune, Misfortune, and Fate: a poor man improves his condition by relying on a lucky niece; Ivan the Unlucky gains luck through marriage; a poor man encounters personified Fortune and Misfortune and receives aid that eventually brings wealth through a fish; and a merchant's son named Luckless is marked and made a compulsory wanderer who receives brief hospitality everywhere.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A poor man wanders in search of a female figure and sees a grey-haired old woman asleep under an oak in a great forest; she proves to be his Luck.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The poor man's Luck tells him that Fate gave him his poor Luck.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Fate is found living at ease in a large house, while her riches wane and her house contracts day by day.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Fate says that her condition at a given hour affects the whole lives of children born at that time, and that the poor man was born at an unpropitious moment.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Fate advises the poor man to take his niece Militsa, who was born at a lucky time, into his house and to call anything he acquires her property; after he follows this advice, things go well with him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When a stranger asks who owns a splendid cornfield, the poor man says it is his, and the crop begins to burn; when he corrects himself and says it belongs to Militsa, the fire goes out and the crop is saved.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Ivan the Unlucky, a peasant, goes to the king for advice about his continual lack of success; the king's nobles and generals cannot solve the matter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The king's daughter says that if Ivan were married, the Lord might allot him another sort of Fortune; the king orders her to marry him, and the marriage brings Ivan good luck.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In a Grodno story, a poor man meets two ladies, one Fortune and the other Misfortune; they give him money twice, but his wife unwittingly gives the money away both times.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The two ladies then give the poor man two farthings and tell him to give them to fishermen and ask them to make a cast for his luck; a fish is caught and brings him wealth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A wealthy merchant's son is so unlucky that after losing his inheritance he works as a laborer and herdsman but causes heavy losses to his masters.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"After the merchant's son nearly burns down the royal distillery, the king pardons him, names him Luckless, orders a stamp set on his forehead, exempts him from tolls and taxes, and orders that he receive food, drink, and lodging wherever he appears but never stay more than twenty-four hours in one place.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"poor man in the first anecdote","description":"A poor man who seeks his Luck and Fate, follows Fate's advice about Militsa, and later saves his crop by naming Militsa as its owner.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"grey-haired old woman, the poor man's Luck","description":"A grey-haired old woman asleep under an oak in a great forest, identified as the poor man's Luck.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Fate","description":"A female figure living in a large house whose riches and house change; she explains how her condition at birth-time affects lives and gives advice to the poor man.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Militsa","description":"The poor man's niece, born at a lucky time, whose nominal ownership of acquisitions protects the poor man's prosperity.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"stranger at the cornfield","description":"A stranger who asks the poor man to whom the splendid field of corn belongs.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Ivan the Unlucky","description":"A peasant known as Ivan the Unlucky who goes to the king for advice about his constant want of success.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"king's daughter","description":"The king's daughter who suggests that marriage might allot Ivan another sort of Fortune and is then ordered to marry him.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"king in Ivan the Unlucky story","description":"The king who consults his nobles and generals about Ivan and then commands his daughter to marry Ivan.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Fortune in the Grodno story","description":"One of two ladies met by a poor man; she is identified as Fortune.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Misfortune in the Grodno story","description":"One of two ladies met by a poor man; she is identified as Misfortune.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"poor man in the Grodno story","description":"A poor man who meets Fortune and Misfortune, receives money and farthings from them, and gains wealth through the resulting fish.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"wife of the Grodno poor man","description":"The poor man's wife, who unwittingly gives away the money he received.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"fishermen","description":"Fishermen who receive two farthings and are asked to make a cast for the poor man's luck.","role_refs":["role:12"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"merchant's son, Luckless","description":"A wealthy merchant's son who loses his inheritance, causes losses in service, nearly burns down a royal distillery, and is officially named Luckless.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"king in the Luckless story","description":"The king who pardons the unlucky merchant's son, names him Luckless, orders him marked, and sets rules for his treatment.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"seeker of improved fortune","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The figure wanders in search of his Luck and then seeks Fate to understand and remedy his poor Luck.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"personified good fortune","assigned_to":["fig:2","fig:9"],"basis":"One figure is explicitly the poor man's Luck, and another lady is identified as Fortune.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"birth-hour fate allocator","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"Fate says her condition at a given hour affects all children born then and explains the poor man's unpropitious birth moment.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"fortunate proxy owner","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Militsa was born at a lucky time, and Fate advises that the poor man's acquisitions be called her property; this practice makes things go well and saves the crop.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"questioning stranger","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"The stranger asks to whom the splendid cornfield belongs, prompting the ownership statement after which the crop burns.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"unlucky sufferer","assigned_to":["fig:6","fig:14"],"basis":"Ivan is known as the Unlucky and lacks success; the merchant's son is so unlucky that his affairs and employments repeatedly fail.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"royal counselor and bride","assigned_to":["fig:7"],"basis":"The king's daughter gives the marriage advice and is then ordered to marry Ivan, bringing him good luck.","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"royal authority","assigned_to":["fig:8","fig:15"],"basis":"One king commands his daughter to marry Ivan; the other king pardons, names, marks, and regulates the treatment of Luckless.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"role:9","label":"personified misfortune","assigned_to":["fig:10"],"basis":"The passage identifies one of the two ladies as Misfortune.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"role:10","label":"recipient of fortune gifts","assigned_to":["fig:11"],"basis":"The poor man receives money and later two farthings from Fortune and Misfortune, leading eventually to wealth.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"role:11","label":"unwitting disposer of gifts","assigned_to":["fig:12"],"basis":"The wife gives away the gifted money without intending to thwart the gift.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"role:12","label":"casters for luck","assigned_to":["fig:13"],"basis":"The fishermen are asked to make a cast for the poor man's luck after receiving the two farthings.","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"oak in the forest","literal_form":"An oak tree in a great forest under which the poor man's Luck sleeps.","associated_figures":["fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":["tree"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"sym:2","label":"fire in the corn crop","literal_form":"Fire that begins to burn the corn crop and then goes out when ownership is restated.","associated_figures":["fig:1","fig:4","fig:5"],"taxonomy_refs":["fire"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"sym:3","label":"contracting house of Fate","literal_form":"Fate's large house, which contracts day by day as her riches wane.","associated_figures":["fig:3"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"sym:4","label":"splendid cornfield","literal_form":"A splendid field of corn that burns when claimed by the poor man and is saved when assigned to Militsa.","associated_figures":["fig:1","fig:4","fig:5"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"sym:5","label":"money gifts","literal_form":"Ten roubles, twenty roubles, and two farthings given to the poor man by the two ladies.","associated_figures":["fig:9","fig:10","fig:11","fig:12","fig:13"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"sym:6","label":"fish bringing wealth","literal_form":"A fish caught after the fishermen make a cast for the poor man's luck, bringing him wealth.","associated_figures":["fig:11","fig:13"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"sym:7","label":"forehead stamp","literal_form":"A stamp set on Luckless's forehead under the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l8696-l8815","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MYTHOLOGICAL. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER III. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 8696-8815","start":"8696","end":"8815","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage explains Russian and Slavic beliefs about Friday as a day associated with a female sacred figure later merged with St. Prascovia, followed by a tale in which Mother Friday punishes a woman for spinning flax on Friday and later restores her sight after repentance. It then introduces a similar Wednesday tradition and begins a tale in which Mother Wednesday appears to a young housewife who invoked her while leaving spinning unfinished.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The commentary says the Russian name Pyatnitsa lacks the mythological significance of Friday or Vendredi, but that Friday was consecrated by old Slavonians to a goddess akin to Venus or Freyja.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The commentary says the Friday goddess became merged in Christian times with St. Prascovia and is addressed as Mother Pyatnitsa-Prascovia.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Mother Friday is said to wander through peasant houses on her holy day and to be offended by certain kinds of work.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The prohibited Friday activities named include women sewing, spinning, weaving, or bucking linen, and men plaiting bast shoes or twining cord.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Spinning and weaving are described as especially offensive to Mother Friday because their dust and refuse injure her eyes; she is said to avenge this with sore eyes, whitlows, and agnails.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Some villagers are said to go to bed early on Friday evening or sweep their floors on Thursday evening to avoid offending St. Pyatinka or Mother Friday.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Popular belief says Mother Friday has sometimes been seen pricked by needles and pierced by spindles used by women who failed to keep the day holy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In the Friday tale, a woman spins flax instead of revering Mother Friday, falls into a deep sleep, and Mother Friday enters in a white dress and stuffs flax dust into the woman’s eyes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After waking, the punished woman is told by other women that Mother Friday has punished her; she begs forgiveness, promises a taper, and Mother Friday later removes the dust from her eyes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The commentary says the Wednesday story is very similar to the Friday story and notes possible explanations for Wednesday traditions, including former heathen holiness or later Christian transfer from Friday.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In the Wednesday tale, a young housewife spins late during the night between Tuesday and Wednesday, sets down her hatchel without crossing herself, and calls on Mother Wednesday to help her rise early and finish spinning.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Mother Wednesday appears before dawn in a lit room, wearing a white towel as a head-dress, preparing the stove and fire, saying she has spun and woven the linen, and commanding the housewife to draw water from the brook.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Mother Friday / Mother Pyatnitsa-Prascovia","description":"A female sacred personification of Friday, associated with an older goddess and St. Prascovia; she wanders houses on Friday, takes offense at prohibited domestic work, appears in a white dress in the tale, punishes a spinning woman, and later removes the punishment.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Woman who spins on Friday","description":"A woman who fails to revere Mother Friday, works flax with a distaff, falls asleep, receives dust in her eyes from Mother Friday, repents, promises a taper, and is restored.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Other women present in the Friday tale","description":"Women who witness Mother Friday’s visit, are frightened, and tell the punished woman what has happened.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Mother Wednesday","description":"A female personification of Wednesday who appears after being invoked, identifies herself as Wednesday, prepares the household fire and stove, says she has spun and woven the linen, and glares angrily at the young woman.","role_refs":["role:1","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Young housewife in the Wednesday tale","description":"A young housewife spinning late at night, who leaves her hatchel without crossing herself, calls on Mother Wednesday, and is frightened by Mother Wednesday’s appearance and commands.","role_refs":["role:3","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Personified sacred weekday","assigned_to":["fig:1","fig:4"],"basis":"Both Mother Friday and Mother Wednesday are addressed as female personifications of named weekdays.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"Enforcer of Friday work taboo","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Mother Friday is offended by Friday spinning and other work and punishes the spinner by filling her eyes with flax dust.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"Domestic worker at risk through spinning","assigned_to":["fig:2","fig:5"],"basis":"Both women are engaged in spinning at ritually charged times connected with Friday or Wednesday.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:6"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"Repentant supplicant","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"The punished woman asks Mother Friday for forgiveness, admits guilt, and promises a taper.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"Restorer after repentance","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Mother Friday returns during the night and removes the dust from the woman’s eyes.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"Witnesses and interpreters of punishment","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"The other women see the event, are frightened, and identify it as Mother Friday’s punishment.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"Invoked supernatural domestic helper","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Mother Wednesday says she came to the housewife’s aid and has spun and woven the linen while preparing fire and stove.","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"Invoker of Mother Wednesday","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"The young housewife calls on Mother Wednesday to help her rise early and finish her spinning.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"Friday as holy day","literal_form":"Pyatnitsa / Friday as a consecrated day on which certain work is forbidden","associated_figures":["fig:1","fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"sym:2","label":"Flax dust in the eyes","literal_form":"Dust and refuse from flax and spinning, placed into the transgressor’s eyes","associated_figures":["fig:1","fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"sym:3","label":"Needles and spindles","literal_form":"Domestic work implements said to prick or pierce Mother Friday when used on her holy In these variants a bean or pea grows from the ground or cottage to heaven, allowing an old man, grandfather, or moujik to climb upward. Some variants end with an old woman’s death, while others continue with a heavenly hut or house, abundant food, goat guardians with many eyes, a sleep charm, expulsion from the upper house, loss of the stalk, a descent by cobweb cord, a fall into a swamp, and rescue by a duck.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The commentator states that the Beanstalk myth is found among many peoples and mentions American and Malayo-Polynesian versions of a heaven-tree story.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The commentator states that European forms are usually crude and fragmentary and that Russian versions are generally preserved as introductions to other stories.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In one Russian version, a girl drops a bean, and the bean grows up to heaven.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In the same version, the old man climbs to heaven, then tries to carry his wife up the beanstalk, drops her, and she is killed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After the wife is killed in the first variant, the old man calls in the Fox as a wailer.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In a Vologda variant, a pea sprouts, grows higher than the house, and produces peas that the old man climbs to gather.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In the Vologda variant, the old man’s bundle of peas falls and kills the old woman.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In another variant, a bean sown under a table grows through the table area, ceiling, and roof until it reaches heaven.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The grandfather climbs to heaven and finds a hut with pancake walls, white-bread benches, and a stove of buttered curds.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Twelve sister-goats enter the hut; they have increasing numbers of eyes from one to twelve.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The grandfather repeatedly uses a charm commanding eyes to sleep, but with the twelfth goat he charms only eleven eyes and is seen and caught by the remaining eye.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In a Munchausen-style variant, a cock finds a pea, the cottager waters it, and the pea grows through the cottage and up to heaven.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The moujik climbs to heaven hoping to see what is there, including sugar and mead, and enters a large wooden house with abundant food.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A seven-eyed goat guards the stove; the moujik charms six eyes to sleep but overlooks the seventh.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The house-master learns what happened, becomes angry, calls servants, and has the intruder turned out of the house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"When the moujik returns to the place of the pea-stalk, the stalk is gone; he makes a cord from floating cobwebs, fastens it to the edge of heaven, and begins to descend.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The moujik reaches the end of the cobweb cord before reaching earth, lets go after crossing himself, and falls into a swamp.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"A duck builds a nest on the moujik’s head, lays an egg in it, and
