markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage gives several Russian and neighboring folk legends: a king consults increasingly older men about an unusually large grain of corn, and the oldest explains past abundance and his own vigor by righteous living; hills and mountains arise when the Devil, after carrying soil in his mouth during the creation of the earth, coughs and leaps while fleeing thunder and lightning; several animal traits and taboos are explained by their origins or actions, including crayfish, the snake that saves Noah's Ark, the horse and ox at the manger, the sole or half-eaten fish, a water-denied bird, sparrows, and swallows.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A king finds a grain of corn as large as a sparrow's egg while roaming with princes and boyars.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The king's followers seek explanations from progressively older men.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The oldest man says he sowed and reaped such corn when he was young and kept some in his granary as a memorial.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The oldest man explains his greater nimbleness by saying he lived according to the law of the Lord and did not grasp at another's property.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In a creation legend, the Lord orders the Devil to dive into the watery depths and bring up soil from the bottom.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Devil takes soil in his mouth as well as in his hand.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After the Lord sprinkles the soil and the flat earth appears, the Devil chokes and flees; hills arise where he coughs, and mountains where he leaps.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Old Ritualists avoid eating crayfish because they hold it was created by the Devil.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A snake is esteemed because it is said to have stopped a leak in Noah's Ark with its head after the Devil, in mouse form, gnawed a hole in it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Horse flesh is considered unclean because the horse ate the hay concealing the infant Saviour, while the ox preserved or replaced it.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Two legends are given for the sole or half-eaten fish: one involving the Queen of the Baltic Sea, and one in which a half-eaten fish comes to life at the Blessed Virgin's condition to Gabriel.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A bird refuses to help carry waters to their appointed places and is then forbidden by the Lord from approaching seas or streams.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A Kharkof legend says the sparrow betrayed Christ's hiding-place by chirruping while other birds tried to draw the seekers away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Other Russian traditions say swallows carried away the nails for the crucifixion, while sparrows brought them back and cried that Christ was living.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The passage gives consequences for birds: killing a swallow is a sin, its nest brings good luck, the sparrow is a bad omen in a cottage, and its legs are invisibly bound so that it hops.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"King","description":"A king who finds the unusually large grain and questions old men about it.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"First old man","description":"An old man scarcely able to crawl on crutches who cannot explain the grain and refers the question to his father.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Second old man","description":"The father of the first old man, limping with one crutch, who says his own father has such seed in his granary.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Patriarch aged one hundred and seventy","description":"The oldest man, walking nimbly without guide or crutch, who says he sowed and reaped the large grain and explains his vigor by righteous conduct.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"The Lord / God","description":"The divine figure who creates the earth from soil, orders waters to be conveyed, and punishes disobedient The passage then comments that powers once attributed to Perun are now ascribed to more than one Christian saint, giving examples of St. George with a lance and St. Andrew with a mace; in a Chernigof legend Andrew destroys a witches' village that had stolen the holy stars, leaving a swamp.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaker markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage surveys legends and rites associated with St. George/Yegory in Russian and related Slavic traditions: his patronage over wolves and livestock, dragon-slaying and saintly roles, spring field and cattle rituals, wolf legends involving allotted prey and miraculous bread, a Gypsy trickster episode involving a golden stirrup, and the beginning of a Bulgarian legend in which pagan Troyan receives gold and silver in place of drinking water.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"St. George is named as Georgy, Yury, and Yegory the Brave, and is described as patron of wolves, flocks, and herds, a Christian Confessor, and a destroyer of snakes and dragons.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage states that differing representations of St. George are explained as legendary ideas from separate sources becoming associated with his name.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In some Russian areas, when cattle first go to spring pastures, a sheep-shaped pie is cut by the chief herdsman and its fragments are kept as a remedy for sheep diseases.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"On spring St. George's Day, fields are sanctified and sprinkled with holy water; in the Tula Government, a similar service is held over wells.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A youth called Green Yegory is dressed in foliage and flowers, carries a lighted torch and a pie to the cornfields, and is followed by singing girls.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In the Green Yegory rite, a circle of brushwood is lit, the pie is placed in the center, participants sit around the fire, and the pie is divided among them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In Little Russia, the wolf is called St. George's Dog, and sheep killed by wolves are not eaten by humans because they are regarded as divinely assigned to beasts of the field.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A man doomed by St. George tries to hide behind a stove, but a wolf transforms into a cat, enters at midnight, and seizes him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A hunter doomed by St. George kills wolves and hangs their skins, but at the fatal hour one skin becomes a wolf and kills him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A poor brother climbs a tree at night and sees St. George and the Lisun with wolves and bread; St. George gives him a remaining loaf that continually renews itself.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A rich brother imitates the poor brother by climbing the tree, but when no bread remains for one wolf, St. George gives the rich brother to the wolf instead.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A Gypsy asks Yegory the Brave to ask God how he should support his wife and seven children; after forgotten promises, he keeps Yegory's golden stirrup as a pledge.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"God's reply is that the Gypsy's business is to cheat and swear falsely; after hearing this, the Gypsy denies having taken the stirrup and Yegory loses it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A Bulgarian legend says that pagan Troyan did not believe in Christ but in gold and silver; the Lord makes its seventy spring-water conduits run with liquid gold and silver instead of water.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"St. George / Georgy / Yury / Yegory A remnant reaches Kaf, and thirty battered birds arrive at the threshold of the Everlasting One. A fiery angel questions them; the Tajidar answers that they seek admission and the fount from which they flow. They are brought before a blazing throne, where a scroll reveals each soul's history. After confession and casting off the old self, they see in the glory a transfigured figure of themselves. A voice teaches that guide, road, sin, remorse, pilgrimage, arrival, and selves are all movements of the One toward itself, like drops returning to the sea and rays returning to the sun.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the Tajidar ceases speaking from a high station, the prospect of the journey produces dread among the birds.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Many birds slip away to woods and nests; others spend their remaining strength in preparation and never depart.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At the first valley, a dark wilderness and a violent wind described as edged with flames or snow freeze the birds' feathers; a multitude rises briefly and then flees, reducing the caravan to less than half.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Further travelers stop, stray, turn back, fall behind, or die from travel, heat, cold, drought, drowning, famine, poison, predators, madness, self-killing, or fighting over grain.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A handful reaches Kaf, described as having feet in the Seven Seas; only thirty damaged birds reach the threshold of the Everlasting One.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A winged harbinger of flame, also called an Angel and Tongue of Fire, asks who the arrivals are, where they came from, and why they have come.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Tajidar answers for the thirty, saying they are diminished and disfigured fractions of being seeking admission at the treasury door.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Angel says that the one they seek does not need a count of beings by quantity or kind, because he is the universal fount of being.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The spokesman asks to see the fount from which they flow and, in seeing it, to lose themselves there.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The thirty are suddenly before a throne and a majesty wrapped in an insufferable blaze that forces down their gaze.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A lightning-like scroll flashes back to each bird the half-forgotten story of its soul; the passage compares this to Yusuf giving his brethren a writing connected with their sale of their brother.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The thirty respond with confession and self-loathing, cast off the rags of carnal self, and are described as reclothed in the soul's integrity.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"When they raise their eyes again, they see in the center of glory a figure of themselves transfigured, and the passage blurs which is seer and which is seen.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A voice says that seeing and being pass through the sun or glass, that apparent selves are fractions of the All, and that drops, atoms, and rays return to their source.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The voice identifies sin, remorse, guide, obstacle, pilgrim, pilgrimage, road, and arrival as itself moving toward ethnographic discussion of Amerindian ritual practices: dance festivals, shamanic healing, altar worship with representative offerings and pictographs, sacrifice, and later syncretic or hybrid tales combining Bible stories with native stories, including the cult of Handsome Lake and Cushing's “The Cock and the Mouse.”","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage describes Amerindian religion as a system for inducing ancients and gods to take part in human affairs and act for worshipers.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Singing, dancing, and festivals are described as universal practices held at appointed times and places, including festivals for rain, thanksgiving, harvest, grasshoppers, green corn, buffalo, bear, and elk.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage states that festivals are fixed at times indicated by signs of the zodiac and that some tribes devise elaborate calendars connected with picture-writings.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Shamanic medicine is described as invoking gods to drive evil spirits from the sick, using music, dancing, and other methods to obtain help from the ancients.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage mentions scarifying, searing, belief in signatures, and charms used as medicine to drive out ghostly diseases.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"An altar is described as a cleared ground space or raised platform in a kiva or assembly-house, around which priests and acolytes gather to pray and perform ceremonies.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Altar-pieces are said to represent the things requested in supplication, including food, water, crystals, rock fragments, honeydew, colored corn, pictographs, clay models, and carved objects.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The passage describes sacrificial worship as a stage in which objects are thought to supply ancients with food, drink, and pleasures, and first portions of consumables are dedicated to gods.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The passage gives Mexico, especially the Nahua or Aztec, as an example where sacrifice was highly developed and human beings were sacrificed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Handsome Lake is described as a Seneca shaman whose The boy goes out with bow and arrows, meets his Gopher grandfather, and receives underground help. The Gopher tunnels to the Bison's vulnerable heart area, exposes a patch of skin, and instructs the boy to shoot it and flee. The boy shoots; the Bison roars, falls, rips open the tunnel with its horn, and the boy escapes into the Gopher's deeper hole.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The little Top-knots gather around the fallen Giant, eat until they reach the top-knot on his He obtains abundant food from the maiden's family, makes simple weapons, instructs the dogs to follow him secretly after the people sleep, departs for a rendezvous near the Black Mountains and the Spring of the Night-hawks, lights a fire, cooks mush, and feeds the arriving dogs at the camp.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The The giant, expecting the War-gods, pretends to be harmless and urges them to pass beneath him. Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma split to either side; Häki Suto tries to catch them but is blinded by the web.
